Prince Miller.

Oh, you want to know about these? Yeah. But Rusty Dime, that was the first band I played with, you know. And he was a cornet player. Yeah, go ahead. He was a cornet player? He was a cornet player. Yeah.

He led the band? Yeah, he led the band. Well, who was the manager? Well, I was the manager, but I turned it over to the violin player, Blunt. That's how I began to get deep. And my sister, she used to take a photo when she died. So I turned it over to Blunt. What's the violin player's name? Blunt. That's the tall fella? Yeah, you know that. Oh. Did they read much or was it mostly by ear?

Did they read much music or mostly by ear? Oh yeah, especially down there was plenty of music from his wedding. And then after they got blue but he couldn't read no music. You remember blue? Yeah. Yeah, he got dead in a parade run.
Who was the clarinet with Wesley Dimes? How was he? No, clarinet. Who was the clarinet player with Wesley Dimes?

Well, we just had one kind of player. So who was he? Who was the clarinet player? Oh, uh, Blind Freddy. Blind Freddy. Yeah. I see. Blind Freddy was a clarinet player at that time. Bass? T-boy. He called him Eddie Gilmore. He called him T-boy. He worked out by T-boy. Let's see. Now uh... Fetty Boo Boo. Yeah, Thumbo. You know, we called him Fetty Boo Boo, but he was...

Now he doesn't ever get a job. We were high piano players. We had to see a father sometime, uh... We called him Professor. Victor Viall. You ever heard him? No, I don't know. He's a sissy father, you know. He's good. You remember him, Victor Viall. He could play with Franky Duce and all of them, you know. But when we get a piano, you didn't hear some of the piano players coming up. No. No. Most of them was good. Yeah. Funny fellas, huh? Funny fellas, huh? Funny fellas, huh? Funny fellas, huh? Says the piano player was funny fellas, huh? He's a sissy. He's a sissy fella. He's good. You remember him, Victor Viall. He could play with Franky Duce and all of them, you know. But when we get a piano, you didn't hear some of the piano players coming up. No. No. Most of them was good. Yeah.
Funny fellas, huh? Funny fellas, huh?

Yeah. Says the piano player was funny fellas, huh? Yeah. Yeah. Most of them like Tony Jackson and all of them, you know, like that. And I forget, there was about five or six of them, you know. They said Buddy Christian was one, but they were right enough. They said he wouldn't, you know. He died like one. Yeah, Buddy Christian. He had plenty women, huh? Yeah.
He had plenty women, huh? Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Need music to make a living.

So did Frankie Dooson need music to make a living? That's all I know was a dude. Never knew him to work. He had so many women to say, but he wasn't much of his act like that. He had no clothes, you know. Then he'd come and tell stories. When you think you're out, he'd go tell your people, you let him the trombone, he'd point it to you. But he said, you ain't home, you go there and get it and say, he told him to come there and get it. But we didn't tell him, you know. We quit him after that, you know. He was quite bigotty too. Yeah, yeah. I used to have plenty of jobs. We'd get a job sometimes for them big, just like cotton exchange, you know. That's how I did. We'd get $25. That's all. We'd be late sometimes. We'd play the star banger. That's all they wanted to play. Now, we'd play that. Sometimes we'd just take your time to put the trombone out and go, ahhh. He got his 25 dollars. I had that job. I had that job for five years. Every Christmas, Eve, and every New Year's Eve. They used to hire us, you know, like that. They had different places. They had Catmister, St. Charles Hotel, the Roosevelt Hotel, the Milano Hotel. There's about two other hotels. It used to be different places sometimes. They were getting a job.
Where did you work with Wesley Dones?

So where did you work with Wesley Dones? Well, we worked all around the city, until we'd give a dance ourselves with the rest of Baton Rouge. And then we got to play the concert. And after that, the right thing we got traded by the old band. And when they got ready to hire, we had so many dates we couldn't make it. So we'd give it to Bob Lyons. And Bob Lyons sent them 75 dollars deposit. And somehow, they wrote back to us and told him they didn't care for him so much he could keep the money, you know. So they said if we couldn't come, they had to get a band. We told them we couldn't make it so they got that band from Nazi. The Scott Band. You ever heard of that band? Yeah, they got that band. They stayed there about three years. We used to work for all these studios down there all the time. And I hold them all the time, you know. And then all these hotels we used to work in, you know. And dance and all, you know. But I was with wrestling. And then the white people, the white people, they had their own music, you know. And we had our own music too. And we'd go there to give us their music to play. That's where they'd catch us, you see. And we could play their music. But some of the things couldn't play their music, so I started playing his music, you know. Instead of staying, he couldn't hold a band by himself. He had two cornet players. He couldn't make it with one.
Ask him who he would use on second cornet.

Who would he use on second cornet? Well, he had Lewis Armstrong. That was the first one. And then after he got Lewis, he had a couple of more, you know. And then Guy Teller come here. Guy Teller was that next to Lewis Armstrong, you know. I was with him a long time too. Guy Teller. Yeah. They said he was, you know, almost good as Lewis Armstrong that time. So he had Guy. Well, Guy left him there and he went to Chicago. Somebody in the middle, wasn't he? Chicago. Yeah. He didn't do so good though. No, they say he didn't. He could drink some liquor, couldn't he? Ooh. Somebody did a band that liked his body gallon. And he'd give it to him, grab a big cup like that and he'd drink it. He'd kiss his speech to his kids. I remember what caused his death. Yeah, that liquor wasn't it? Liquor and tea. Oh, yeah, yeah, yeah. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
Why not? Ask me if you knew shots.

Did you know shots? Shots, huh, Ruby? I was playing with him. Shots played with us in the full place. I was playing with him. Shots was another liquor-head, too. He was a good corner player, but he was a liquor-head. Shots drank so much whiskey to the kids. He played with us until he got kind of sick. And he wasn't sick so long before he died. He was a good corner player, Shots. Which band was that? Whose band? Well, we was a make-up band, I thought. We didn't have no special name. Then I was with, uh, called it the John Casman band at that time. And we had Wooden Joe. You ever heard of him talking? Wooden Joe and Albert Nickerson, that's his cousin. And Joe was named Nickerson, too, but we used to call him Wooden Joe. He wasn't much, you know, Wooden Joe. He said anything, only one kid. He was so strong. Woo! He could, but I think they called him Wooden Joe. He could blow so alive and blow so long, you know.

. And we had this fellow, William Padjo. You can get him. Yeah, yeah. We had him, right? He was going to school at that time. But he was a good reader, but he couldn't jazz. So we got Ricard Ellis. And then Willie Edwards, we had Willie Edwards. Then we had George McCullen for a little while. I forget this fellow. I wanted to spell it, but I thought I could remember. Du Conger. I couldn't make it out.
Ask him, Du Conger.
Du Conger? Yeah, yeah, Du Conger. Yeah, yeah, Alba Du Conger.
First name?
Alba. You know him, eh? You heard talk of him. Alba Du Conger. They tell me the policeman in Chicago.
First was Wesley Dunn. Yeah, and second was Blue. Yeah. And third was who? What's the man this? No, ask him who the third corner.

Who was the third corner player? William Padjo. William and Ricard Ellis was the fourth. Oh, huh. And then Willie Edwards was the fifth. George McCullen was the sixth. Albert Du Conger, he was the seventh. Chris Kelly, he was another good corner player. You hear what I'm talking about? And then I played by the fellow with the third. Did you play with Jack any?

Huh? You played with Jack some time, huh? Jack? Oh yeah. Yeah, I remember his band when you remember. But you quit him and you taken all that from him, you see? And we went with you. And you know how the two down there was Linton come saying that's bad, well that's how it broke us up, you see? And then we got together and we worked with different other fellas. That's what broke his bad enough, you know? Yeah, I had a job in the country for Austin and Johnny Henry. And then it was Crowback. And he couldn't come to eat. You remember Crowback, don't you? Yeah. He was a clownist player in the psych. And then you remember Kit Harris? Remember him, eh? Johnny Harris, you know? Who was Crowback? And then Cato Harry, big, big, big, big, big. Yeah, I know him. Yeah. And then there was Peter Boquet.
Ask him who was Crowback.

He said who was Crowback? Crowback was a saxophone player. For about seven years, he looked something like a white boy, you know? What was his last name? What was his last name? Crowback? That's his last name, Crowback. I forget his first name. I forget his first name. How many things? Huh? Yeah. He said he forget his first name. Who did he play with? He had much to carry with us a lot. Who did he play with? Crowback. Crowback. He was playing with us. We had, you know, this is making up a band. Sometimes we were high, and when I was with Tom I was, kid I was in the Bronx band. We were high, you know. We were high, you know. And, and I played with Peter Boquet with a band too, you know. But he didn't last long. Then Mud Carter, he come with us for a while. Then he left, went back, and he come back and played with Jack. That's where he come in after he left then. And then Mud Carter, he had a band of himself. And this fella I can't think of. King or someone? Well I just said that to make me remember. King, tell him King.
King Clayton?

Clayton, yeah. King Clayton, yeah. King Clayton, yeah. King Clayton for a while. Mm-hm. And then I played with Lewis Dorman band. Mm-hm. And Auguste Dush . I played with Sam Morgan for a good while. Mm-hm. I played a little while with Joe Howell. And that kid Howell I played with him- I mean Joe Howell I played with him for a little while because he had Frankie Duce in there with him. That's right. The boys wouldn't stick with him on account of Frankie Ducey, we all quit. He had a good band too. The kid Howard, I played with them wrists a little while, you know. Hey, did you know much about Chiff? Chiff? Chiff did. I know it. I know it. Did you play much with him? Yeah, you know, around there, actually, Uri, Uri fired him and his brother, you know. Stomp. Then we used to hire him there. We used to hire him there. Then he left and went to Alexander. And what come old man Paul Bin? Paul Bin? I didn't know what would come of him. He used to play with us sometimes too. Then old man Petit, he used to play with us. Then Morris, you know Morris? French? French, yeah. He used to play with us too sometimes. French, yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Ask him who was in the band when Muck Carey was in the band, I'd be. Right. Yeah, when he finishes there. Then I, uh. He said who was in the band when Muck Carey was there?

He was with Jack when he come with him wasn't he? Something was mad all down there you know. Sip of lettuce you know. And he died you know. He had to stop playing.
And the drummer? Chinese. You said Chinese.
Yeah, you mean with Jack then? Yeah. He played bass. You never heard of him man. Who was the drummer? Chinese? Chinese, yeah. No piano? No.
No.

Duck Earness. Yeah. I played with his band a good while he called his band a young tuccedent. That's where we met over in Ball Oakland remember that time? a young tucceder. And that's where we met over in, over in, uh, Milwaukee, remember that time? And, uh, I had been over there with Doug Ernest, so he hired us again, but Doug had another band, and he turned me over to him. But I went and got butter for tea, you know, and all of them, and Pierre, Earl Luffin, Eric Scott, and then George, uh, uh, George. Washington? No, not George Washington.
What instrument? What instrument he played?

Who, uh, George. George? George, he played drums. Oh. I see if I can say to the last name. George, uh, I mean. George Evans. George Evans, yeah. His mother's Papa Foot, huh? I mean, he's such a son, George. And he died too.
Who's Papa Foot?

So we went over there, the brothers looked at us, you know. He was playing music. Punch and, uh, Brother Petit, they were his buddies, you know. And you know, when we meet on the valley, that's what they call it sometimes, by advertising, we buck against one another. And so they say, Kid Punch over here. And the man got scared, you know. He said, he kept me looking at us, and he said, uh, he said, now it's the same band here, Andrew. I said, they playing out there, but we got a better band this time. He said, yeah, he said, but Kid Punch coming, he said. He said, well, we buddy, you know, what we going to do. So, well, we went on, you know. And when we meet, we play one-two, then we drive off. And we go, and we were buddy, we always, you know, we was buddy, you see. We didn't buck against one another. And then when we got, uh, they closed parts of them down. They couldn't make that. And we had so many people that we couldn't get in that part. Then they came over, and they played a couple of turns, you know. Let's see. Bud Bruchey, you know what I mean? He's an old bass player. Uh, uh. Who did he play with? Yeah, I used to play with him too. Who did he play with? Who he had with him? Bud Bruchey. He had me, his Fostham, Fostham brother, and, uh.
That's Dude and Fostham?

Huh? Dude and Fostham? Yeah, Dude and Fostham, yeah. I forgot about him, but I met him with Fostham. Then I played with their band a good little while too, Fostham band. And then when they get together, when they pick out their best musicians, you know. And they're taking me, Ivers, and Ivers, uh, Martin. He's there too. He's been there before the drummer. Yeah, uh-huh. And then we went to Kid Island. And I left Kid Island. I played Kid Island about two years. Then I told him come and got me on a job to go to Mexico. And, well, I told Alan we was going over there, but not to stay. So he told me, all right, when you come back, your job will be right there. So we went over to stay three months. Then when he came back, I went with him, you know. I went back to the island. Then after a while, uh, uh, Fasher, not Fasher, uh, what's that stuff in there? It's P. on the boat. You remember? Sean? The P. on the fair had a job on a steamy carpenter.
Fats P. Sean?
Huh? Fats P. Sean? No, not Fats. Steve Lewis? Huh? Steve Lewis? No.
Fait Marble.

Fait Marble. Yeah, yeah. Fait Marble, yeah. Fait Marble, yeah. He had it. They came that the honor of the boat was king to faith. I know. So that's when he hold a job so long. Well, I just prayed for him. And he came out into St. Louis. Mm-hmm. Not the island got to St. Louis, but he decided to leave his father, you know, and go to New York. And that broke all the band up, you see. So we all tried to get us. I wanted to go back to Mexico, but my mother's taken sick and die. I never did go back to Mexico, you know. I never did go back to Mexico. Jimmy Dave, he's taken our job away from us. You know, the governor was running out. Oh, he took his job? After they couldn't get us to work, Jimmy Dave would take it, you know. He's been playing over there ever since.

Where did Mutt Carey go when he left Jack? He was in Chicago, California. Went back over there. I think he come back here and died, I think. Know he died up there? California. Oh yeah, that's right, yeah. He was with the kid over there, I think. You know Eddie Gordon, didn't he? He was a good little bass. Me and him was the first one to let's take a hot. Too hot, huh? Yeah. They didn't put it out if you want. No, brother. It's just so hot as ever for me, sometimes I had to make it put it on the radio. I'm going to play there. I'll get it.

Okay. All right, all right. Well, who took Mutt's place? I want to get that straight. I'm the first one. Yeah, well Punch took Mutt's place, so that was 1919. Yeah, that's right. That's when Mutt Carey left. That's when I come in. And you had been playing with Duck, huh?

I played two jobs, I think, with Duck. That's two. What did you say, Mr. McHugh? Huh? What did you say? I tell him I played two jobs with Duck on the side front, then I come with Jack Carey. Yeah. It's just to stop up there and pick you up in races, you know what I mean? Yeah. And your faces coming in the back.
Well, I asked him who he played with right before he played with Jack.

He said, who you played with before you played with Jack? Let's see. What's that with Jack? I had a kind of a big role in Robichaud's, John Robichaud's band. So that means- And then, you know, John Robichaud had a Spanish band, good, you know. And he used to play for all the rich white people. And now and then he would play for the college when they had a tag. And so, he kind of went down during the length. So his drummer, I was playing with his drummer. There was four or five piece band, Walter Blunder. You got any? Yeah, he was best around there on drums. Clionette there, he put out the drum and played clionette. But then after he got us with John Robichaud, he was playing drums there. And Charlie McCurdy, he learned, he learned how to play clionette. Then when he learned how to play clionette, when he dropped drums. And that put Robichaud's band to the band, because people had got kind of tired of his band. And that's where I went with him. Yeah, I went with Joe Howard's band, but I didn't stay with him long, you know. And then I went with Bob Lyon. I didn't stay with Bob Lyon too long, because Bob was so crooked, you know. And then from there, I worked with Sam Morgan. I stayed with Sam Morgan too. Sam kind of lost or losing his mind then, you know. And then we were just scrapping up bands, you know. And way after a while, I tape organized a band, you know. We were playing down the distance then, you know. And then I tape got me rid of it. I stayed with him about two years, playing on one job. Then I left him there, I went with my wife's cousin, Ernest Poirier. I don't know if he got in there, saxophone there. I went with him, stayed with him a long time. Yeah.
Big George Williams. Yeah. I hear him in the street with Big George.
Big George Williams, eh? Yeah.

Maurice. Yeah. And I know you ought to have Maurice Duran, eh? Yeah, he's in California now. Yeah. He played with us a good while too, Maurice. Which band? Who Maurice worked with out there? Huh? They went up there for two years, you see? They went up there for four months. They went up there for four months.

segments.title: Recording date, address and names
segments.summary: Vincent and the interviewers establish the date (3 Dec 1959), the address and who is present; Vincent is asked to talk about people on a sheet.

segments.title: Rusty Dime's band, first band; manager Blunt and who read music
segments.summary: Vincent's first band was led by cornetist Wesley Dimes; he managed it then handed it to violinist Jasper Blunt. Most of the band read music except the drummer.

segments.title: Clarinet, bass and piano players with Dimes; early pianists
segments.summary: He names the clarinetist (Blind Freddy), the bassist T-Boy, and talks about pianists such as Victor Viall, Tony Jackson and Buddy Christian.

segments.title: Frankie Duson and hotel New Year's jobs
segments.summary: Remarks on Frankie Duson's habits, and the band's yearly Christmas and New Year's Eve jobs at hotels paying $25.

segments.title: Where the Dimes band worked; playing for white dances
segments.summary: They played dances around the city and handed overflow jobs to other bands; Vincent describes playing white people's music versus their own.

segments.title: Second cornet: Louis Armstrong and Guy Kelly
segments.summary: Dimes' second cornetists included Louis Armstrong and then Guy Kelly, who left for Chicago and died after heavy drinking.

segments.title: Shots, the John Casman band and Wooden Joe
segments.summary: Vincent recalls cornetist Shots Madison, a pick-up band called the John Casman band, and Wooden Joe Nickerson's powerful blowing.

segments.title: Ranking the cornet players in the Dimes band
segments.summary: Vincent lists cornetists in order: Dimes, Blue, William Padjo, Ricard Ellis, Willie Edwards, George McCullen, Alba Du Conger, plus Chris Kelly.

segments.title: Playing with Punch and Jack Carey; Crowback and others
segments.summary: Vincent describes the break-up when Punch Miller took over Jack Carey's band, and the sidemen around it, including saxophonist Crowback and Peter Bocage.

segments.title: Long list of bands played with
segments.summary: He runs through bandleaders he worked under: King Clayton, Lewis Dorman, Sam Morgan, Joe Howard and others.

segments.title: Who was in Jack Carey's band; bass, drums, no piano
segments.summary: Asked about personnel when Mutt Carey was in Jack Carey's band: a bassist, drummer Chinee, and no piano; pianos were not used then.

segments.title: Joe Welch and Duck Ernest's Young Tuxedo band
segments.summary: Vincent recalls violinist Joe Welch and playing with Duck Ernest, whose band included drummer George Evans.

segments.title: Bucking Kid Punch; Bud Brunies and the Fostham band
segments.summary: He tells how bands advertised against each other and stayed friendly, then lists bands he joined including Fostham's.

segments.title: Kid Island's band, Mexico job and Fate Marable
segments.summary: Vincent played about two years with Kid Island, went to Mexico, and describes Fate Marable's boat band breaking up and Jimmy Dave taking the job.

segments.title: Where Mutt Carey went; Eddie Gordon on bass
segments.summary: Mutt Carey left for California; Vincent recalls bassist Eddie Gordon.

segments.title: Punch replaces Mutt Carey; Vincent joins Jack Carey
segments.summary: The interviewer confirms Punch took Mutt's place in 1919; Vincent played two jobs with Duck then joined Jack Carey.

segments.title: Bands before Jack Carey: Robichaux, Joe Howard, Bob Lyons, Sam Morgan
segments.summary: Vincent's earlier jobs: John Robichaux's band, Joe Howard, Bob Lyons (crooked), Sam Morgan, then Ernest Poirier; Maurice Durand later moved to California.

segments.title: Robichaux's cornetist Kimball, Thetto Harris, Lewis Nelson
segments.summary: Robichaux's cornetist was Kimball; Vincent discusses sidemen who came and went, including Thetto Harris and Lewis Nelson.

segments.title: Robichaux band: guitarists, clarinetists and drummer
segments.summary: Returning to Robichaux, he names the guitar player before him, clarinetist Charlie McCurdy, a successor, and drummer Reed Happy.

segments.title: Robichaux trombonists: Vic Gasper and Johnny Lindsey
segments.summary: Names the Robichaux trombone players and clears up Johnny versus Joe Lindsey, who played with Pierron.

segments.title: Pianists with Robichaux and the Hippolyte Charles band
segments.summary: Robichaux had Kimball's wife on piano at the Lyric; Vincent then names members of Hippolyte Charles's band.

segments.title: Sorting out bassists Eddie Dorsey and Eddie Jackson
segments.summary: A back-and-forth to establish which long-tall bass player Eddie is; Jackson dead, Dorsey alive.

segments.title: Sam Morgan's band: Alfred Williams, T-Boy and the bass
segments.summary: Vincent recalls Sam Morgan's band, Alfred Williams, Alfred Martin and bassist Eddie Gilmore (T-Boy), who stuck together.

segments.title: Young Morgan Band and Transcena's banjo test at Spanish Fort
segments.summary: A story of the boss Transcena sitting by banjo players and firing one, and how Vincent survived by chording up the neck.

segments.title: When banjo players started making ninth chords
segments.summary: Vincent says he used ninths after banjo and guitar parts appeared in orchestra music, after World War I; Keto played them and a pianist tested him with chords.

segments.title: Ninths before the Depression; leaving for Alexandria
segments.summary: Asked if ninths predate the Depression, he says yes, then recounts working in a big band in Alexandria and being tied by a debt.

segments.title: Ninths in Mexico and with Jack Carey; keeping in practice
segments.summary: He played ninths in Mexico in 1926 but not with Jack Carey; he has not touched his banjo in a year due to illness.

segments.title: Diminished and augmented chords and how he learned them
segments.summary: He learned chord symbols from banjo and guitar parts, taught himself, and played diminished and augmented chords before knowing their names.

segments.title: Elevenths, thirteenths and minor sevenths
segments.summary: Elevenths and thirteenths came in after the Depression; minor sevenths and diminished chords were used on tunes like Sophisticated Lady.

segments.title: Buddy Petit as first to run diminished chords on trumpet
segments.summary: Vincent says Buddy Petit was the first trumpeter he heard using such chords and variations, and was a good musician who drank wine.

segments.title: Joe Petit and Buddy Petit's upbringing and teacher
segments.summary: Joe Petit was Buddy's stepfather; Buddy was actually named Joseph Crawford and had perfect notes and an unknown teacher.

segments.title: Buddy Petit's augmenteds, elevenths and flatted fifths
segments.summary: Buddy made augmented and minor sevenths chords on tunes like High Society; the interviewers also ask about flatted fifths locally.

segments.title: Tape runs out
segments.summary: The tape ends and the recorder is turned off.

segments.title: Buddy Petit's odd chords versus Chris Kelly's plunger style
segments.summary: Buddy played slow pieces with odd chords, unlike Chris Kelly who played straight with a plunger; Bunk Johnson-style cigarette paper pads mentioned.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet and the Victor Ballroom jams
segments.summary: Vincent played mandolin with Bechet at the Victor Ballroom at Lafayette and Rampart, where musicians jammed upstairs.

segments.title: Jazz Baby, his brother Julius Benson and the Mamie Smith show
segments.summary: Vincent talks about his brother Julius Benson and Jazz Baby, and a planned show with Mamie Smith that fell through.

segments.title: Dr. Ernest's band and Robert Taylor; Fuchs's big feet
segments.summary: After Duck, the band included Robert Taylor; Vincent names clarinet, drums and a bass drummer who died on parade, with an aside on a shoemaker named Fuchs.

segments.title: Locating the ballroom at Lafayette and Rampart
segments.summary: The interviewer asks where they used to jam; Vincent places it at Lafayette and Rampart.

segments.title: After Duck: the six-piece band with T-Boy
segments.summary: He and T-Boy formed a six-piece band with Chani and others; later he played with Buster Moore and Richard Batiste.

segments.title: Batiste, Amos Riley and the clarinets
segments.summary: Clarifying the order of Batiste and Amos Riley; Vincent talks about clarinet keys and Willie Humphrey.

segments.title: Amos White's Creole Jazz Band, then Alexandria
segments.summary: After his band broke up he joined Blind Freddie and Amos White; light-skinned players, T-Boy on bass; then Amos left north and Vincent went to Alexandria.

segments.title: Who he played with when times got tough
segments.summary: The interviewer rephrases the Depression question as 'when times got tough'.

segments.title: Carnival and circus life, a storm that killed performers
segments.summary: He toured in small shows through Louisiana, Texas and Mississippi, and survived a storm that killed performers by cutting through the tent.

segments.title: Poverty on the road and going back to day work
segments.summary: He made little money on the road, then returned to the white family who raised him for yard and house work.

segments.title: Vermilla and Joe Johnson the trombonist
segments.summary: He does not know Vermilla; the interviewers identify a trombonist, Joe Johnson, from Algiers who worked with him.

segments.title: Johnson the clarinetist and the Mexico trip
segments.summary: A clarinetist named Johnson went to Mexico with them; the band was short on good men and lost Walter Brundy.

segments.title: Bob Thomas, trombonist
segments.summary: Vincent comes up with Robert Thomas, a trombonist now sick.

segments.title: Lucci Jackson and young players like Vic Dispenza
segments.summary: He doesn't recall Lucci or Albert Jackson, and mentions a young reader, Vic Dispenza's son.

segments.title: Working with Red Allen and a band in Mexico
segments.summary: When Red Allen needed a band, Vincent assembled one with George Lewis and others and went to Mexico, where dance halls got rowdy.

segments.title: Shooting out the lights in dance halls
segments.summary: Vincent describes drunk patrons shooting the lights out in dance halls.

segments.title: Celestin's Tuxedo and Maple Leaf bands, as described by a visitor
segments.summary: A second speaker recalls Celestin's Original Tuxedo and Maple Leaf bands alternating with Piron, and names Tio and Charlie Bocage.

segments.title: Which band swung best or kept steadiest time
segments.summary: Asked which band had the most swing or steadiest time, Vincent says Alfred Williams on drums kept time like a clock.

segments.title: Charlie the piccolo drummer; trailing off
segments.summary: A visitor mentions a drummer who blew piccolo in street parades; the tape trails off.
